children: By Victoria Albert, Suzanne Kapner and Joseph Pisani
A powerful Nor'easter has forced Macy's to reschedule its Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City.

Officials made the decision to wait until Saturday over safety concerns. The giant balloons that are the marquee attraction of the annual holiday celebration are only permitted to fly when winds are under 23 mph and gusts don't exceed 34 mph.

The National Weather Service said it expects winds of roughly 25 to 35 mph in the area with gusts reaching up to 60 mph on Thanksgiving. It warned the winds could topple trees and power lines, with widespread power outages expected.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said Wednesday.

The decision is a disappointing turn for the parade, which is celebrating its 100th march this year, and the thousands of visitors it brings to the city. Along with tourists who line the 2.5-mile parade route from Manhattan's Upper West Side to Macy's flagship store in Midtown, marching bands and other performers come from all around the country to participate.
Jill Paragi was in disbelief when she heard about the postponement and kept pointing to a patch on the back of a red Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade jacket she was wearing that said "Rain or Shine!"
"I bought this for nothing," Paragi, 55 years old, said of the jacket she got through Macy's website two months ago.
Paragi, who came to New York City with her sister and two friends, is headed back to Pittsburgh Friday.
"We're going to miss the parade now," said Paragi's friend, Joyce Miklos, 61. "Well, unless they delay our flight. Which is always a possibility."

This year's lineup is set to feature 100 inflatables, including a 33-foot-long Hello Kitty and a "Despicable Me" minion riding a giant banana, in addition to the mainstays: intricate floats, high-school marching bands and themed clowns.

The parade has been canceled three times before, in 1942, 1943 and 1944, due to a rubber and helium shortage during World War II. The balloons have only been grounded once, in 1971, when a 63 mph gust was recorded in Central Park.

The inflatables are a beloved feature of the parade. In the early years, the balloons would simply be released into the skies at the parade's end, with Macy's offering a $100 reward for their safe return. At least one, a giant blue hippopotamus, was never found, the retailer said.
That practice ended in the 1930s, after a 22-year-old student aviator tried to capture a cat-shaped balloon with her biplane and plunged into a dive over Queens. Now, volunteers deflate them.

But as long as the balloons have been flying, they have been vulnerable to blustery conditions. Occasionally, the results have been disastrous: At the 1997 Thanksgiving parade, heavy winds pushed a "Cat in the Hat" balloon into a lamppost, which fell and injured four spectators. One person was in a coma for 24 days.

Macy's estimates that more than 3.5 million people watch the parade in-person each year, and 35 million more tune into the 3.5-hour broadcast. Revelers have at times withstood extreme weather to attend in-person, including a frigid 2018 parade day where temperatures dropped as low as 17 degrees.
